Today through Tuesday night: Shortwave ridging of higher pressure 
will build in over the Inland Northwest today. Temperatures will 
rebound with highs back into the 80s this afternoon. Smoke is still 
present in the vicinity of fires burning in the Cascades, 
particularly in Chelan County. The warmer weather coming up may 
result in increased fire activity for the short-term and a bit more 
smoke for those communities in the Wenatchee Area, especially around 
Chelan. The ridge axis begins to shift east of the region on Tuesday 
with a longwave trough of lower pressure digging down off of the 
west coast. This will back the flow pattern advect even warmer 
temperatures in from aloft. Most areas will see their warmest 
temperatures on Tuesday, particularly across northeast Washington 
into the northern Idaho Panhandle with temperatures warming into the 
mid to upper 80s. A shortwave disturbance rounding the longwave 
trough will punch through Oregon and into southeast Washington by 
Tuesday afternoon. Increasing moisture and destabilizing mid levels 
in the atmosphere will bring a 15% chance for thunderstorms over the 
Northeast Blue Mtns into the Palouse, L-C Valley, Camas Prairie, and 
southern to central Idaho Panhandle. Dry low levels will mean that 
any thunderstorms will bring strong outflow wind potential. 
Convective activity will continue into the overnight hours on 
Tuesday into Wednesday morning with the threat of thunderstorms 
expanding into northeast Washington and into North Idaho. Moisture 
also will increase with showers and thunderstorms expected to become 
progressively wetter.

Wednesday through Thursday night: A more fall like weather pattern 
is in store for the latter half of the workweek. The trough of low 
pressure off of the coast continues to dig and closes off with and 
pushes across an occluded front Wednesday night into Thursday. 
Southerly winds will increase over the Columbia Basin and up the 
Okanogan Valley ahead of the front for Wednesday afternoon. Winds 
will be a bit gusty between Moses Lake to Omak and Oroville with 
gusts up to 30-35 mph. This may pick up a bit of dust across the 
area. how much blowing dust occurs will depend on shower activity 
with the first shortwave Tuesday night into Wednesday.

Precipitation along the occluded front looks to be substantial. It 
will be widespread in areal coverage and be wetting. All areas will 
see a 60% chance of at least a tenth of an inch from Wednesday night 
through Thursday afternoon. The Cascades, northern mountains, 
extreme eastern Washington and the Idaho Panhandle will see a 
greater than 70% chance for at least a tenth of an inch of rainfall 
over this period, and these same areas will see a greater than 50% 
chance of at least a quarter of inch of precipitation. The prospect 
of this much rain will be very welcome sight and at least place a 
figurative wet cloth on our active fires burning across the region. 
Temperatures will cool down quite a bit as well with high 
temperatures down into the 60s and low 70s by Thursday. All of the 
moisture with cooler temperatures will bring the potential for fog 
to develop at least in the sheltered valleys.

Friday through Monday: Models are trending toward the closed low 
being cut off from the Polar Jet over the weekend. This leads 
considerable more uncertainty as where the center of the low sets up 
will determine temperatures and precipitation chances. The general 
consensus is the low will cutoff and retrograde a bit, and could 
drift far enough west to set up off of the coast. This possible 
scenario would deliver more moisture into the region, but also would 
result in temperatures rebounding a bit with increased instability 
and the potential of thunderstorms. Another scenario is the low sets 
up more so over the Inland Northwest keeping temperatures cooler and 
below normal. Warmer temperatures and better instability would then 
more likely take place east of the area over western Montana. /SVH
